outline.theme: Mysuru is a city that holds its celebrations and its wounds together, balancing royal grandeur with ancient curses and historical scars.
outline.hook: A queen stands at the edge of the Kaveri river, her hands empty of the temple jewels that the new rulers of Mysuru wanted. Before she steps into the water, she speaks a curse that will shape the next four hundred years of the city's royal house.
outline.gap: How does a royal family that built one of the grandest palaces in Asia survive a curse that denies them natural heirs?
outline.bridge: We all build beautiful things to show the world we are fine, even while carrying a quiet worry we cannot quite shake.
outline.peak: In 1897, in the middle of a royal wedding, the old wooden palace catches fire and burns to the ground, forcing a queen to rebuild not just a home, but a statement of survival.
outline.ending: The lights on the palace walls flicker out, leaving only the dark outline of the hill watching over the quiet city.

chapters.title: The Two Stories of the City
chapters.hook: Look at the palace in front of you on a Sunday night when nearly a lakh of electric bulbs turn on at once.
chapters.gap: Why does this city of light keep an image of a cursing queen inside its most sacred royal rooms?

beats.text: Mysuru runs on two stories: one is the electric glow of ninety-seven thousand bulbs, and the other is a dark curse from a queen who went into the river.
beats.label: history

beats.text: People here say that in 1610, Queen Alamelamma cursed the Wadiyars to never bear children, and indeed, the family has repeatedly had to adopt its heirs.
beats.label: legend

beats.text: The family takes this so seriously that they still honour an image of her inside the palace, even though geologists say the sand that buried her town was just wind and river movement.
beats.label: history

chapters.title: The Demon and the Goddess
chapters.hook: If you look up at the hill rising over the city, you are looking at a battlefield named after the loser.
chapters.gap: Why would a proud city name itself after a monster instead of the goddess who saved them?

beats.text: The story goes that a buffalo demon named Mahishasura ruled this land until the goddess Chamundeshwari killed him on that very hill.
beats.label: legend

beats.text: Historians argue the name Mysuru simply comes from an old term for buffalo country, but the city still keeps a bright, painted statue of the demon on the road up the hill.
beats.label: disputed

beats.text: The palace faces east, looking directly at the temple on the hill, so the kings could look at their protector every morning.
beats.label: history

chapters.title: Out of the Ashes
chapters.hook: In 1897, the smell of burning wood filled the air as the old palace went up in flames during a royal wedding.
chapters.gap: How do you build a palace that can never be burned down by fate or fire?

beats.text: The regent queen, Kempananjammanni, refused to build with wood again and hired British architect Henry Irwin to design a palace of stone, iron, and glass.
beats.label: history

beats.text: If you stand in the wedding hall and look up, you will see a ceiling of turquoise and green stained glass made in Glasgow, held by Scottish iron pillars pretending to be stone.
beats.label: history

beats.text: This grand stage was designed for the Dasara festival, with wide roads planned specifically for elephants to march from the palace to the parade grounds.
beats.label: history

chapters.title: The Tiger and the Soap
chapters.hook: A mechanical tiger chewing on a British soldier sits in a London museum, a quiet reminder of a time when Mysuru fought back with iron and fire.
chapters.gap: How did a kingdom known for its fierce rockets end up famous for sweet Mysore pak and fragrant sandalwood soap?

beats.text: Tipu Sultan used iron-cased rockets against the British before his defeat in 1799, after which the British took his mechanical tiger as a trophy.
beats.label: history

beats.text: When the Wadiyars were restored, they turned to trade; during the First World War, when sandalwood could not be exported, the king decided to make soap instead.
beats.label: history

beats.text: Today, the city smells of that sandalwood soap and the sweet Mysore pak created by a palace cook named Madappa, proving that while the kingdom's weapons are in foreign museums, its tastes remain here.
beats.label: history

### Scores and Problems

**Scores:**
*   **Hook:** 4/5. The opening sentences create a strong contrast between the brilliant lights and the dark curse, though a tired traveler might find the phrasing a bit dry.
*   **Theme:** 5/5. The theme of balancing celebration and wounds is consistently maintained throughout.
*   **Specifics:** 5/5. Excellent use of checkable facts (97,000 bulbs, 1610, Talakad, Chamaraja Wadiyar X) and sensory details (electric glow, cold river water, sand).
*   **Peak:** 4/5. The peak occurs around the second paragraph with the dramatic curse, which is close to the two-thirds mark but could be paced slightly better.
*   **Ending:** 4/5. The image of the dark hill is good, but it feels a bit abrupt.
*   **Honesty:** 5/5. The draft clearly distinguishes history from legend and cites its sources accurately.

**Three Biggest Problems:**
1.  **Curiosity Gap Timing:** The curiosity gap about the queen's image inside the sacred royal rooms is opened in the first paragraph but is partially explained too early in the second paragraph, weakening the tension.
2.  **Repetitive Phrasing:** The draft repeats the fact about the royal family adopting heirs in both the second and third paragraphs, which wastes word count and disrupts the flow.
3.  **Lack of Reader Bridge:** The draft attempts a bridge in the first paragraph ("We all build beautiful things..."), but it feels abstract rather than connecting directly to a physical sensation or common experience the reader has right now.

Specifics: 4/5. Good specifics (Mahishasura, Chamundeshwari, sword, cobra, moustache), but lacks sensory details like smell or touch.
Peak: 2/5. The peak is missing; the text ends flatly on a description of the palace facing east.
Ending: 2/5. Ends on a dry geographical observation about picking out the temple tower on a clear morning.
Honesty: 5/5. The labels are correct, and the facts are cited properly.

Three biggest problems:
1. **Weak Hook and Curiosity Gap**: The opening does not start with a person, a contradiction, or a question. It fails to open a clear curiosity gap early that is closed near the end.
2. **Lack of Narrative Drive (People, not lists)**: The draft describes statues and palace orientations rather than a person wanting something and meeting an obstacle.
3. **No Bridge to the Reader's Life and Missing Peak**: There is no relatable connection to the reader's own life, and the story lacks a dramatic peak two-thirds of the way through.

Three biggest problems:
1. **Theme dilution**: The draft starts with the wound of the fire but forgets the "celebrations and curses" theme by the third paragraph, focusing instead on urban planning and elephants.
2. **Missing the core conflict**: The draft ignores the city's most famous wound and celebration contrast: the electric lights of the palace sitting alongside the dark, 400-year-old royal curse.
3. **Weak peak and ending**: The story ends quietly on a dark hill rather than peaking on the dramatic tension of the family's survival against a curse, and lacks a strong final image.

### Scores and Problems

*   **Hook**: 4/5. The opening image of the mechanical tiger is strong, but the second sentence ("How did a kingdom...") is a rhetorical question, which slightly weakens the immediate narrative pull for a tired traveller.
*   **Theme**: 4/5. The theme of balancing grandeur with wounds is present, but the transition between the military defeat of Srirangapatna and the commercial success of soap/sweet-making feels slightly disconnected rather than fully integrated.
*   **Specifics**: 5/5. Excellent use of checkable facts (Tipu, Srirangapatna, 1799, 1916, Madappa, Alamelamma) and sensory details (iron-cased rockets, smell of sandalwood, flickering lights).
*   **Peak**: 3/5. The peak (the curse of Alamelamma) is introduced too late and resolved too quickly in the second paragraph, missing the two-thirds mark for maximum dramatic tension.
*   **Ending**: 4/5. The image of the flickering lights and the dark hill is strong, but it feels a bit abrupt.
*   **Honesty**: 5/5. The legends are correctly framed ("The story goes..."), and historical facts are properly cited.

**Three Biggest Problems:**
1.  **Curiosity Gap and Peak Placement**: The curiosity gap about the city's dual nature (celebration and curse) is opened but not given enough space to breathe. The peak—the curse of Alamelamma—is rushed at the very end of the draft rather than peaking at the two-thirds mark.
2.  **Rhetorical Question in the Hook**: The second sentence uses a rhetorical question ("How did a kingdom..."), which violates the house style's preference for direct, active narrative drive and can alienate a tired reader.
3.  **Flow and Connection to the Reader**: The bridge to the reader's own life is somewhat abstract ("We all build beautiful things..."). It needs to connect more tangibly to the physical reality of standing in Mysuru today, looking at the palace.

facts.title: Two stories run this city
facts.body: Mysuru runs on two stories. One is electric: on Sunday nights, close to a lakh of bulbs come on across the palace at once, and for about an hour the whole building is drawn in light. The other is much older and much darker, and it involves a queen, a river, and a curse that the royal family has taken seriously for four hundred years. You will hear both before this walk is done. Keep them in your head together, because that is the trick of this city. The lights are for everyone. The curse is family business. Mysuru has always known how to hold a celebration and a wound at the same time.

facts.title: The palace city that kept its capital manners
facts.body: Mysuru is the city the old Mysore kingdom was named for, and it still carries itself like a capital. For most of five centuries the Wadiyar kings ruled from here or from Srirangapatna, sixteen kilometres north, and when the British handed the state back to them in 1799 they put the court in this city and kept it here until 1947. So what you get is a royal town built with a plan and a budget: a palace at the centre, wide straight roads leading off it, a hill with a temple watching over everything, and the Kaveri feeding the plain around. Bengaluru took the government. Mysuru kept the palace, the festival, the silk, the sandalwood and the pace.

facts.title: The tiger that eats a soldier
facts.body: Tipu Sultan called himself the Tiger of Mysore, and he meant it. His throne had tiger heads. His soldiers wore tiger stripes. And he owned a life-sized mechanical tiger shown mauling a British soldier. Turn a handle and the soldier's arm flails while an organ inside makes the man wail and the tiger grunt. It was equal parts toy, propaganda, and threat. When Srirangapatna fell in 1799, the British took it home as a trophy, which is its own kind of irony. The machine sits in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London today, still working, still mid-bite, one of their most visited objects. Mysuru's anger, on permanent display in England.

facts.title: The wrestlers train through the night
facts.body: In the old quarters of this city there are garadi mane, earthen wrestling houses, and men still train in them the way they did when the palace paid for it. The floor is red earth mixed with oil and turmeric, turned over before each session. The Dasara wrestling tournament is the surviving public face of it. If someone offers to take you into a garadi at five in the morning, go. You will see rope climbing, stone weights, and a form of wrestling with rules older than the Wadiyars. Ask before you photograph. These are training halls, not exhibitions.

facts.title: A buffalo demon gave the city its name
facts.body: Ask anyone here how the city got its name and you will hear the same story. The story goes that a demon called Mahishasura, a buffalo with a man's cunning, ruled this land and terrorised everyone in it. The gods could not touch him, so the goddess Parvati took the form of Chamundeshwari, came down to the hill above the city and killed him there. The land was Mahisha's town, Mahishuru, and centuries of speech wore that down to Mysuru. Historians will tell you the region was called buffalo country long before any demon, and that the name probably comes from the animal, not the villain. The city does not mind. It kept the demon's name, put the goddess on the hill, and celebrates her winning every autumn.
facts.source_name: Devi Purana tradition and Mysore historians, general reference

facts.title: The adoption record, without the curse
facts.body: Set the curse aside and look at the record. The Wadiyar succession has repeatedly gone sideways rather than straight down. Krishnaraja Wadiyar the Third had no surviving son and adopted. Chamaraja Wadiyar the Tenth came to the throne by adoption. Jayachamarajendra Wadiyar, the last ruling maharaja, had a son, but the line after him passed by adoption again in 2015. That much is documented. Sand did cover Talakad, and geologists put it down to the river shifting course and wind moving dune fields. Two true things sitting next to each other is not the same as one causing the other. The family itself has treated the curse seriously, which is also a fact.

facts.title: Rockets before the British had them
facts.body: Tipu's army used iron-cased rockets. Not fireworks. Tubes of soft hammered iron packed with powder, strapped to a bamboo shaft, fired in volleys at ranges over a kilometre. They were used against the British at Pollilur and again at Srirangapatna. After 1799 the British collected the wreckage and took it home, and William Congreve worked from it to develop the Congreve rocket, which the Royal Navy then used. The line runs from this island to the rockets in the American national anthem. Some of the recovered casings are in the Royal Artillery collection in England.
facts.source_name: Royal Artillery Museum collection, general reference

facts.title: One family, six hundred years, two interruptions
facts.body: One family has been attached to this city since 1399, when a chieftain called Yaduraya took charge of Mysuru for the Vijayanagara empire. The Wadiyars stayed feudatories until that empire fell, then took Srirangapatna in 1610 and ruled as kings in their own right. Two interruptions matter. From about 1760 the general Hyder Ali, and then his son Tipu Sultan, held the real power with a Wadiyar kept on as a figurehead, until the British stormed Srirangapatna in 1799 and Tipu died in the fighting. The British then put a Wadiyar child of four on the throne and moved the court back to this city. The maharajas ruled, under British oversight, until independence in 1947, and the family still lives in the palace.

facts.title: An entire city was designed as a stage
facts.body: Look at how wide the roads are here compared with any other Indian city of this age. That is deliberate. Mysuru was laid out under the Wadiyars and their engineers with the Dasara procession in mind: a fixed route from the palace to the Bannimantap parade ground, wide enough for elephants and crowds, with sightlines to the palace and the hill. The lakes, the parks and the public buildings were placed around it. You are walking through a piece of nineteenth-century urban planning built to hold one ten-day event, and it holds the rest of the year as a side effect.
facts.source_name: Mysuru city planning history, general reference

facts.title: An island with a short temper
facts.body: Srirangapatna is an island. The Kaveri splits, goes around the town, and joins itself again, which is exactly why Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan made it their capital. Water is a wall you do not have to build. For decades this small island held off the most powerful army on earth. It fell on the fourth of May 1799, when British troops broke through the fortifications, and Tipu died fighting in the breach rather than surrendering. The spot where his body was found is marked, and it is an oddly quiet place for somewhere that ended an era. The whole island is a battlefield wearing a town.

facts.title: Butter dosa, no menu required
facts.body: There is a small place in Nazarbad called Vinayaka Mylari, and it has been making essentially one thing for decades: a soft, spongy dosa finished with a spoon of butter, served with a coconut chutney and nothing else worth mentioning. You do not really order. You indicate a quantity. The dosa arrives folded, pale gold, and lighter than it has any right to be. They open early, and the queue builds after nine, so make it your breakfast rather than your brunch. There are two Mylari shops near each other and a long-running family disagreement between them. Locals have opinions. Both are good. Pick the shorter line.

facts.title: The city ran on electricity before most of Europe
facts.body: In 1905 Mysuru became one of the first cities in Asia to get street lighting from hydroelectric power, drawn from the Shivanasamudra falls on the Kaveri about a hundred kilometres away. The transmission line was among the longest in the world at the time. The Maharaja lit the palace with it, which is where the illumination tradition you see on Sundays begins. So the bulbs on the palace are not a modern tourist display bolted on later. They are the surviving habit of a state that treated electricity as a public statement.
facts.source_name: Kaveri hydroelectric scheme records, general reference

facts.title: Why this city smells of sandalwood
facts.body: During the First World War, Mysore's sandalwood suddenly had nowhere to go. Europe, the biggest buyer, had other concerns. Stocks of the fragrant wood piled up, and the king of the day, Krishnaraja Wadiyar the fourth, decided that if the world would not buy the wood, Mysore would sell the soap. A factory came up in 1916, and Mysore Sandal Soap has been in production ever since, more than a hundred years now. You will smell it in the market, in the shops, in half the hotel bathrooms in this city. A world war, a trade problem, and a king who liked chemistry. That is the recipe.

facts.title: The sweet the palace cook had no name for
facts.body: Mysore pak is this city's sweet, and by tradition it was born in the palace kitchen. The story told at Guru Sweet Mart, at the edge of Devaraja Market, is that a royal cook called Kakasura Madappa put gram flour, ghee and sugar syrup together for a maharaja who wanted something new, and had no name ready when asked, so he called it after the city and the syrup, paka. His descendants still make it in that shop, and the ghee-heavy version that melts rather than crumbles is the one to buy. Eat it the same day. Around it the city eats well and early: a Mysore masala dosa with red chutney spread inside, a plate of idli at a tiffin room, and filter coffee poured from a height.

facts.title: Three palaces burned before this one
facts.body: The palace in front of you is the fourth one to stand on this ground. The one before it was mostly wood, and in 1897 it caught fire in the middle of a royal wedding. The family got out. The building did not. The regent queen, Kempananjammanni, decided there would be no more wooden palaces, and gave the job to Henry Irwin, the British consulting architect down in Madras. Stone, iron, and glass this time. It took fifteen years. So when you walk in, remember you are walking through someone's answer to a fire. Look for how little wood there is.

facts.title: More people come here than to the Taj Mahal
facts.body: Here is a number that surprises people. This palace draws visitor figures in the same range as the Taj Mahal, and in some years it has been reported ahead of it. Most of those visitors are Indian, and most of them are from Karnataka. That changes what you are standing in. This is not a monument that foreigners discovered and locals tolerate. It is a place families come to on a Sunday, in their good clothes, with children who have been told the stories on the bus. Look at the crowd around you as much as at the building. The crowd is the point.

facts.title: The queen who went into the river
facts.body: In 1610, a widowed queen named Alamelamma was pursued to the banks of the Kaveri at Talakad. The new rulers of Mysuru wanted the temple jewels in her keeping. The story goes that she stood at the edge of the water and cursed them before she went in. Let Talakad turn to sand. Let Malangi become a whirlpool. Let the kings of Mysuru never bear children. Talakad today is buried under dunes of sand. And the Wadiyar family has, generation after generation, adopted its heirs. Inside this palace there is an image of Alamelamma, and the family honours it to this day. Make of that what you like. They did not take chances.

facts.title: The demon in the city's name
facts.body: The story goes that this region was once terrorised by a buffalo demon named Mahishasura, and that the goddess Chamundeshwari fought him on this hill and killed him. The place became Mahishuru, the town of Mahisha, and the centuries wore that down into Mysuru. So the city is named after the loser of the fight. On the road up the hill you will pass a huge painted statue of the demon himself, sword in one hand, cobra in the other, moustache immaculate. Locals treat him with a certain fondness. Without him, after all, the city would need another name.

facts.title: The Dasara procession painted on the wall
facts.body: In the long corridor there is a set of oil paintings that show the Dasara procession as it looked in the 1930s. Walk along them slowly. You are looking at a crowd portrait. The artists painted real people, and many of them are recognisable to families in this city even now. Follow the line of elephants. The one carrying the golden howdah is the point of the whole thing. In those days the Maharaja rode in it. Since 1971 the howdah carries the idol of Chamundeshwari instead. The route in the painting is still the route the procession takes today.

facts.title: The double-headed bird over the gate
facts.body: Look at the arch above the main gate. There is a bird with two heads on it. That is the Gandaberunda, the emblem of the Mysore kings. In the old stories it is a form Vishnu took to absorb the force of another god who had gone too far. Two heads, one body, enough power to hold something no single creature could hold. You will start seeing it everywhere once you have noticed it: on the palace, on state buses, on the emblem of Karnataka. The Wadiyars used it for centuries. So does the state government today.

facts.title: Dasara begins on this hill
facts.body: For ten days in autumn this hill is the start of the whole festival. The goddess is worshipped here first, and only then does the city below light up. The procession that everyone photographs, the elephants and the golden howdah, is the closing act on the tenth day. Before 1971 the Maharaja rode in that howdah. Now the idol of Chamundeshwari rides in it and the family walks behind. The change happened when the royal titles ended. The ritual did not stop. It transferred from the king to the goddess he served.

facts.title: Stand under the peacocks
facts.body: In the Kalyana Mantapa, the wedding hall, most people look straight ahead and keep moving. Stop instead, and look up. The ceiling is stained glass, turquoise and green, worked into peacock patterns, and it was made in Glasgow along with the cast iron pillars holding it up. Scottish foundry work, shipped across the sea, to sit above Mysuru weddings. Then move to the side of the hall and look at a pillar up close. It is iron pretending to be carved stone, and it pretends well. The whole room is a conversation between two places that never met.

facts.title: The left row of the Durbar Hall
facts.body: The Durbar Hall is where the king sat in public, and everyone photographs it from the centre. Do not stand in the centre. Walk to the left-hand row of pillars and look down the length of the hall from there. The arches line up, one inside the next, and the painted ceiling runs above them like a scroll being unrolled. This is the angle the hall was designed to be seen from, the view a courtier would have had while waiting. From the middle you see a big room. From the left row you see a stage.

facts.title: Why the palace faces the hill
facts.body: Stand at the front of the palace and look east. That hill with the temple on top is Chamundi. The palace faces it directly, and that is deliberate. Chamundeshwari is the family goddess of the Wadiyars. The city takes its name from a demon she killed. So the arrangement is simple: the ruling house built its home looking at the goddess who protects it. On a clear morning you can pick out the temple tower from here. During Dasara the two places work as one event, the hill in the day and the palace at night.
